newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Oil-for-food deal in trouble after Kurdish crisis.
newsitem.headline: Oil-for-food deal in trouble after Kurdish crisis.

text.p: By sending its troops into Kurdish provinces, Iraq may have jeopardized an oil-for-food deal aimed at easing the impact of devastating trade sanctions on the Iraqi people.
The United States, as well as other Security Council members, insist the plan will not be a casualty of the current crisis but they differ in predicting its future.

Attempting to summarize the Security Council's views, British envoy Stephen Gomersall said on Tuesday a withdrawal of Iraqi troops from the northern Kurdish areas they entered was necessary before it could sell limited quanities of oil.

"A return to the status quo is indeed a prerequisite for the implementation of the (plan) which all members of the council restated that they wish to see implemented as soon as conditions permit," he told reporters.
Nevertheless, there are fears the status quo may be defined differently by the United States and Britain compared to other members, such as Russia and France.

Diplomats recalled that Washington, which co-sponsored the resolution setting up the program, single-handedly delayed its approval by insisting on tighter controls as well as coming up with last-minute proposals during the negotiations.

At issue is a May 20 accord between Iraq and the United Nations that permits Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil in order to purchase badly-needed food, medicine and other goods for its people suffering under six years of sanctions.
About $260 million was earmarked for the Kurdish provinces in the north, not under Baghdad's control and where the United Nations was to distribute the supplies.
The deal was first offered to Iraq several years ago but President Saddam Hussein refused, partly because of funds set aside for the Kurds which he said violated sovereignty.
On Tuesday, President Bill Clinton noted that the Kurdish city of Arbil, which was seized by Iraqi troops, was a key distribution center for the humanitarian aid.
"Until we are sure these humanitarian supplies can actually get to those who need them, the plan cannot go forward, " he said.
At the State Department, spokesman Nicholas Burns said "It's going to be some time before we can get back to any consideration of that program."
And at the United Nations, the deputy U.S. ambassador Edward Gnehm, explained that the United States still wanted to see the program carried out.

But he said "it is a statement of fact that there is a new situation on the ground and it is inevitable that the United Nations must look at what has been agreed to so the food and humanitarian goods go to the people it is meant for."
"It has been iraqi behaviour that has determined answers as to the timing," he said.

Russia's ambassador, Sergei Lavrov, said implementation of the program was up to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who should continue working toward putting it into force "bearing in mind the safety of international personnel."
Before the Iraqi offensive in the north, the plan awaited only assurances from Boutros-Ghali that all arrangements were in place.
But the secretary-general announced on Sunday that he was postponing implementing the program, planned for this month because of fears about the safety of U.N. staff.
